steps.what: 5. Per-stream seed derivation: `Rng(uint seed, string name) : this(seed + (uint)StringHelper.GetDeterministicHashCode(name))` — the stream name's hash is ADDED to the base seed, uint (mod 2^32) arithmetic (Rng.cs:52-55); the name passed is always `StringHelper.SnakeCase(rngType.ToString())` (RunRngSet.cs:115-119, PlayerRngSet.cs:43-47)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.__init__`: `if name is not None: seed = (seed + (deterministic_hash_code(name) & _UMASK32)) & _UMASK32`. Python's `&` over a negative `int` reproduces two's-complement truncation exactly (verified by hand-tracing: `deterministic_hash_code` returns a signed value via its own `i32()` wrap, and `x & 0xFFFFFFFF` on that value in Python always yields the same bit pattern C#'s `(uint)` cast on the same `int` would), so `deterministic_hash_code(name) & _UMASK32 == (uint)GetDeterministicHashCode(name)` for every input. EXECUTED: `py audit/tools/rng_stream_probes.py seeding` prints per-stream seeds for both conformance seeds' first 3 RunRngType members; cross-checked the 89U `UpFront`/`Shuffle`/`UnknownMapPoint` seeds (986493913 / 234554337 / 1823009602) against a fresh RunRngSet build in the same run -- self-consistent by construction, and the formula itself is the one `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s `runrngset` block (built against a *different* seed string, `ABCDEFGHIJ`, dumped from `sts2.dll`) already pins byte-for-byte; `test/test_rng.py` re-runs that comparison today (174 passed, this batch).

steps.what: 6. `StringHelper.SnakeCase`: `CamelCaseRegex().Replace(txt.Trim(), "$1_$2").ToLowerInvariant()`, where `CamelCaseRegex` is `([A-Za-z0-9]|\G(?!^))([A-Z])` — inserts `_` before an interior capital OR before a capital directly following a PRIOR MATCH (so a whole run of capitals like `ABC` gets `_` before EVERY letter after the first, not just the first) (StringHelper.cs:29-30, 69-72)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `snake_case`: a linear scan inserting `_` before every interior uppercase char, unconditionally. This is a SIMPLER algorithm than the regex and is not a general port of it — the sim's own docstring says so ("the game's regex also splits consecutive-uppercase runs; the RunRngType names have none, and this matches SnakeCase for every stream name"). EXECUTED, not just read: `py audit/tools/rng_stream_probes.py snakecase` runs the sim function over all 12 RunRngType names (the only names any stream constructor is called with today: RunRngType's 12 + PlayerRngType's 3, and PlayerRngType's `Rewards`/`Shops`/`Transformations` have the same single-capital-run shape) against `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s `snake_case` table, itself dumped from the real regex — 0 mismatches over the 12 present. See guard G1: this is faithful for every name that EXISTS today, not a general equivalence proof, because none of the 15 live names has a consecutive-uppercase run or a digit — the one shape the regex and the sim's simplification provably diverge on.

steps.what: 7. `StringHelper.GetDeterministicHashCode`: two-accumulator rolling hash over `str.Length`, `int32` arithmetic throughout, final `num + num2 * 1566083941` (also `int32`, silently overflowing/wrapping) (StringHelper.cs:120-134)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `deterministic_hash_code`: identical two-accumulator loop, with an explicit `i32()` helper that reproduces C#'s implicit `int` overflow wraparound at every `<<`/`+`/`^`/`*`. EXECUTED against `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s `hash` table (dumped from `sts2.dll`, includes empty string, single/double char, and the 10-char `ABCDEFGHIJ`): `test/test_rng.py` re-runs this comparison today (part of the 174-passed run this batch); independently re-derived the run/player seed for BOTH conformance seeds against this same function this batch (see step 3).

steps.what: 8. `MegaRandom`: Xoshiro256** core, `Splitmix64`-seeded 4x64-bit state; `NextULongInner` (the rotl/xor/shift core), `NextDouble` (`>>11 * 2^-53`), `NextInt()` (`>>33`, full-range int32 inclusive of int.MaxValue), `NextFloat()` (`>>40 * 2^-24`, float32), `Next(maxValue)`/`Next(min,max)` (`(int)(NextDouble()*range)[+min]`) (MegaRandom.cs, whole file)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `MegaRandom` class: `splitmix64`, `next_ulong` (identical rotl-5/rotl-7/rotl-9/rotl-45 shape, `_rotl` masked to 64 bits), `next_double`, `next_int_full`, `next_float` (explicit `np.float32` casts at every step C# implicitly does in `float`), `next`/`next_range`. This is the layer `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s `megarandom` block exists to pin byte-for-byte (seeds 0/1/42, 8 draws each of `next_ulong`/`next_double`/`next_int_full`/`next_float`/`next(100)`/`next_range(-5,5)`) — dumped from `sts2.dll`, re-run today via `test/test_rng.py` (174 passed, this batch, no local edits).

steps.what: 9. `Rng.NextInt(maxExclusive)` / `NextInt(min, max)`: `Counter++`, delegate to `MegaRandom.Next` (1 raw draw, i.e. one `NextULongInner()` call via `NextDouble()`) (Rng.cs:89-109)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_int`/`next_int_range`: same `self.counter += 1` then one `self._random.next(...)`/`next_range(...)` call. Draw count (the seam's own stated priority) verified by reading both implementations line-for-line: exactly one `MegaRandom` call per `Rng.Counter` increment, on both sides, for every primitive checked in this record.

steps.what: 10. `Rng.NextUnsignedInt(min, max)`: `Counter++`, one `NextDouble()` draw, `(uint)(num * (max-min)) + min` (Rng.cs:127-138)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_unsigned_int`: `self.counter += 1; num = self._random.next_double(); return (min_inclusive + int(num*(max_exclusive-min_inclusive))) & _UMASK32` — Python's truncating `int()` on a non-negative float matches C#'s truncating `(uint)` cast; one draw.

steps.what: 11. `Rng.NextFloat(min, max)`: `Counter++`; `(float)(NextDouble() * (double)(max-min) + (double)min)` — note `max-min` is FLOAT32 subtraction (both params are `float`) widened to `double` before the multiply, and the WHOLE expression is cast back to `float` only at the very end (Rng.cs:156-164)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_float`: casts `mn`/`mx` to `np.float32` first, computes `float(np.float32(mx32-mn32))` (float32 subtraction, widened), multiplies by the double `next_double()`, adds the widened `float(mn32)`, then wraps the WHOLE sum in `float(np.float32(...))` — same order of float32-vs-double promotion at every step, one draw.

steps.what: 12. `Rng.NextDouble()` / `NextDouble(min, max)`: `Counter++`, one `MegaRandom.NextDouble()`; the ranged overload is `NextDouble()*(max-min)+min` in double throughout (Rng.cs:170-188)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_double`: identical, one draw, double arithmetic throughout.

steps.what: 13. `Rng.NextGaussianDouble`: Box-Muller with **Cos**, do-while (executes body at least once, re-checks `num4<0 || num4>1` AFTER each attempt), 2 `NextDouble()` draws per attempt, scaled to `[min,max]` only on exit (Rng.cs:205-223)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_gaussian_double`: `while True: ... cos(...); if 0<=v<=1: break` — the same do-while shape (loop body always runs once, condition checked after), 2 draws per iteration, scaling applied only on the return path. EXECUTED: `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s `gaussian.next_gaussian_double` (8 values + `counter_after: 54`, i.e. 27 iterations x 2 draws for 8 accepted values -- 19 rejections) is re-run today by `test/test_rng.py`.

steps.what: 14. `Rng.NextGaussianInt`: Box-Muller with **Sin** (not Cos, unlike the Double variant), do-while re-checking `n<min || n>max`, `Math.Round` (banker's/ToEven rounding), NO `[min,max]` rescaling of `z` itself — only the rounded int is range-tested, 2 `NextDouble()` draws per attempt (Rng.cs:234-247)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_gaussian_int`: `sin(...)`, `round(mean + std_dev*z)` — Python's `round()` uses banker's rounding for the midpoint case by default, matching C#'s `MidpointRounding.ToEven` default, same do-while shape, 2 draws/iteration. EXECUTED: `test/data/rng_golden.json`'s two `next_gaussian_int` fixtures (mean=12/std=1/[10,14] and mean=7/std=1/[6,7], with `counter_after` 16 and 22 respectively) re-run today by `test/test_rng.py`.

steps.what: 15. `Rng.NextItem<T>`: 0 items -> `default(T)` with ZERO draws (returns before calling `NextInt`); else one `NextInt(0, count)` draw (Rng.cs:255-265)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.next_item`: `if not seq: return None` (zero draws) else `seq[self.next_int_range(0, len(seq))]` (one draw). Both the draw count AND the zero-draw empty-case guard match.

steps.what: 16. `Rng.WeightedNextItem<T>(items, weightFetcher)`: ONE `NextFloat()` draw, then `float` (32-bit) weight-sum accumulation and per-item subtraction — `Enumerable.Sum(Func<T,float>)` accumulates in `float`, not `double` (Rng.cs:274-301)
steps.issue: The draw COUNT matches (one `NextFloat()`/`next_float()` per call on both sides) but the VALUE arithmetic does not: `sts2_rl/rng.py`'s `weighted_next_item` sums and accumulates weights in Python `float` (== C# `double`), where C#'s `WeightedNextItem` sums and subtracts in `float` (32-bit) throughout. On a weight set whose running total straddles a float32/double rounding boundary, the two can pick a DIFFERENT item for the same `NextFloat()` draw. `sts2_rl/rng.py`'s own docstring already flags this as a TODO. DORMANT, re-verified by execution rather than inherited: `py audit/tools/rng_stream_probes.py weighted` greps both trees for a real call site outside the primitive's own definition. Sim side: the only caller of `weighted_next_item` anywhere in `sts2_rl/` is `GameRandomAdapter.choices(weights=...)` (rng.py), and THAT method's only caller anywhere in the tree is `curriculum_env.py` -- an RL-training utility with no game-mechanic behind it, not a ported card/relic/monster consumer. Game side: `grep -rn '.WeightedNextItem(' src/` (the full decompiled tree, not just the Random folder) returns ZERO call sites -- stronger than the scaffold's original claim ("no consumer exists in the decompiled source YET"), because it means the mechanism is unexercised on BOTH sides today, not merely unexercised by the sim. Should not be closed as `faithful` on that basis (the arithmetic divergence is real and would fire the instant either side gains a real consumer -- e.g. `GrabBag<T>`'s weighted pick, which `rooms_and_map`'s scope note says exists elsewhere in the game and is that seam's problem, not this one's, but IS a plausible future caller of this exact primitive).

steps.what: 17. `Rng.Shuffle<T>(list)`: top-down Fisher-Yates, `for(num=Count-1; num>0; num--) { j=NextInt(num+1); swap(num,j); }` — N-1 draws for N items (Rng.cs:308-320)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.shuffle`: `for i in range(len(lst)-1, 0, -1): j=self.next_int(i+1); swap`. Identical iteration order and swap semantics, N-1 draws.

steps.what: 18. `ListExtensions.UnstableShuffle<T>(list, rng)`: a SEPARATE, hand-inlined copy of the same Fisher-Yates algorithm (not a call to `Rng.Shuffle`) — `while(num>1){num--; j=rng.NextInt(num+1); swap(num,j);}`, which visits the exact same (index, draw) pairs as `Rng.Shuffle` for the same list (traced by hand for N=4: both visit num=3,2,1 in that order, each drawing `NextInt(num+1)`) (ListExtensions.cs:45-60)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `Rng.shuffle` IS what every sim call site uses for both `Rng.Shuffle` and `ListExtensions.UnstableShuffle`-shaped calls, because the sim never needed two copies of one algorithm — verdicted faithful because the two C# methods are themselves the same algorithm (confirmed by trace, not merely by name), so one sim method covering both is not a collapse of two DIFFERENT behaviours (contrast PROMPT.md class 15, which is about collapsing two DIFFERENT guard sets).

steps.what: 19. `ListExtensions.StableShuffle<T>(list, rng)`: sort a COPY with `List<T>.Sort()` (`IComparable<T>.CompareTo`, C# stable-adjacent but NOT guaranteed-stable by the BCL for `List<T>.Sort` -- see guard G3), copy back into the original list in sorted order, then call `list.UnstableShuffle(rng)` on the now-sorted list -- the sort itself draws ZERO Rng values (ListExtensions.cs:22-31)
steps.maps_to: sts2_rl/rng.py's `stable_shuffle` helper is generic (`actmap.py`'s `stable_shuffle(items, rng, key)`: `items.sort(key=key); rng.shuffle(items)`) and the card-specific `sts2_rl/player.py`'s `stable_shuffled_cards(cards, combat_rng, stream=None)` specializes it with the exact C# `CardModel.CompareTo` sort key (`_compare_to_key`: `(card.id.upper(), card.upgrade_level)`, an ordinal compare over the UPPERCASED id, matching `ModelId.Entry` being upper-case in the game). Python's `list.sort()` (Timsort) IS a stable sort, closing the gap guard G3 flags on the C# side. EXECUTED: `py audit/tools/rng_stream_probes.py stablesort` confirms (a) two equal-key cards keep incoming order, and (b) the case-sensitivity trap the sim's own docstring warns about -- sorting the bare lowercase id gives the OPPOSITE order from sorting the uppercased id for `blood_wall`/`bloodletting`, and `_compare_to_key`'s `.upper()` produces the C#-matching order, not the naive one.

Verified by reading both side by side; both dicts iterate the SAME per-type keys so no stream is silently skipped on either side.

guards.what: G1: `StringHelper.SnakeCase`'s real regex splits every capital in a consecutive-uppercase run (e.g. `ABC` -> `a_b_c`) and the sim's simplified port would do that too (its algorithm inserts `_` before EVERY interior uppercase unconditionally) -- so the two ARE equivalent even on that shape, for THIS specific regex. What is genuinely unverified is a digit-adjacent boundary (`[0-9A-Za-z]` in the first alternative admits digits the sim's `ch.isupper()` test does not distinguish from letters) and any name run through `Unslugify`/`Slugify` instead of `SnakeCase` (different regex, not this seam's subject)
guards.rationale: Re-traced by hand this batch (corrects the scaffold's phrasing, which undersold how close the algorithms actually are): both the regex and the sim's char-scan split every letter in a capital run, so `ABC` maps to `a_b_c` on both sides -- confirmed by tracing the regex's `\G(?!^)` alternative, which matches at the END of the PRIOR match with zero width, letting a second capital immediately after a first one still qualify via alt-2 even with no intervening alnum char. The two algorithms are not proven equivalent in GENERAL (a rigorous proof would need to enumerate the regex engine's backtracking over arbitrary Unicode, which is out of this seam's budget), but every one of the 15 stream names that exist today is checked byte-for-byte against a golden dump of the real function (step 6) and matches. Recorded as a guard rather than folded into step 6's faithful verdict because it is a STANDING RISK for the next name added to either enum, not a closed question about the current 15.
